definition: Embellish means to decorate or adorn with ornamental details.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word embellish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know embellish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The luthier embellished the guitar's soundhole with a ring of inlaid mother-of-pearl.
To accent something is to add one small touch — a single ribbon on a plain box; it stops well short of embellish.
Encrust goes further than embellish — ornament piled on ornament until the original surface disappears beneath the crust.

Gild means to coat something with a thin layer of gold — one exact, literal treatment. Embellish is the umbrella above it: adding ornamental extras of any kind for beauty's sake. Every gilded edge is embellished, but you can embellish with thread, paint, or iron and never touch gold.

Festoon means to drape something with garlands, chains, or streamers — ornament that hangs and swings. Embellish is broader and quieter: it covers any decorative addition, including detail stitched, carved, or painted flat onto a surface, where festooning always leaves something dangling.

Garnish is the kitchen's word for ornament: a sprig of parsley or a twist of lemon set on a finished plate. Embellish does the same job everywhere else — gowns, gates, manuscripts — and it can pile on far more than a single finishing touch.

Reporters crowned the senator's ninety-year-old mother the belle of the inauguration ball.
Embellish means to decorate or adorn with ornamental details.

For the mayor's centennial visit, the ironworker embellished the plain park gates with curling vines, oak leaves, and a pair of hammered copper wrens — by unveiling day, visitors were photographing the gates instead of the park.
Embellish is more particular than 'decorate': it means adding ornamental extras to something already complete, purely to make it richer to look at.
The gates worked fine before; the vines and wrens are embellishment.
The word stretches to stories, too — a fisherman embellishes a tale with details that were never there.
Use embellish when extras are added for beauty's sake — needlework, ironwork, the margins of a manuscript — or when a storyteller improves on the truth.
Plain decorate does everyday duty; gild and festoon name particular kinds of embellishing.
And note the quiet warning in the story sense: an embellished account is prettier than what actually happened.

When the town commissioned a mural for the new library, the painter Ana Reyes finished the central scene in a single week.
Then she spent a month on the edges.
She chose to embellish the border with tiny emblems of local life -- a rowboat, a thimble, a line of geese -- each no bigger than a thumbprint.
Critics later argued the mural would survive without a single one of them, and Reyes cheerfully agreed.
The extras were never structural, she said; they were a gift, ornament added purely for the pleasure of the people who would stand close.
